nameStory: The chimney swift earned its name from its modern love affair with human-built chimneys, where it builds its unique stick-and-saliva nests. Before European settlers arrived with their chimneys, these birds nested in hollow trees, but they quickly adapted to take advantage of these perfect vertical "artificial caves" that we built for them.
description: The chimney swift is a sleek, cigar-shaped bird that spends almost its entire life in the air, swooping and diving after flying insects. About the size of a large sparrow, it's covered in sooty gray feathers that give it an almost charcoal-like appearance. These aerial acrobats have incredibly long, curved wings that make them look like tiny boomerangs slicing through the sky. You'll rarely see one sitting still, as their tiny feet can only grip vertical surfaces—never flat ones like typical perching birds.

idTips.label: Boomerang-shaped silhouette
idTips.description: In flight, the bird's body appears as a short, thick cigar with long, curved wings that create an unmistakable boomerang or crescent shape against the sky

idTips.label: Constant flight behavior
idTips.description: Never seen perching on wires, branches, or flat surfaces—only glimpsed clinging to vertical walls or disappearing into chimneys at dusk

idTips.label: Sooty gray coloring
idTips.description: Uniformly dark gray-brown plumage that looks almost charcoal-colored, with no distinctive markings or patches of different colors

idTips.label: Rapid, erratic flight
idTips.description: Flies with quick, stiff wingbeats followed by gliding, constantly changing direction as it chases insects—much more erratic than swallows

idTips.label: Chattering calls
idTips.description: Makes rapid, high-pitched chattering or twittering sounds, especially when multiple birds are feeding together over open areas

habitat: Chimney swifts are most common in towns and cities throughout New England, where chimneys provide nesting sites. You'll see them swooping over neighborhoods, parks, and open areas near human settlements, from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains. They're particularly abundant around older residential areas with traditional brick chimneys.

seasonality.spring: Chimney swifts return to New England in late April or May, when you'll first hear their chattering calls and see them investigating chimneys for nesting sites.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season—swifts are constantly visible during daylight hours, swooping after insects and making their distinctive calls. Watch chimneys at dusk to see them dive in for the night.
seasonality.fall: Birds begin gathering in larger flocks before migrating south in September, creating impressive aerial displays as dozens feed together.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England—these birds migrate to South America and spend the entire winter in the Amazon basin.

funFact: Chimney swifts can't walk or hop because their legs are so short and weak—if one accidentally lands on the ground, it may be unable to take off again and could starve, since it needs to drop from a vertical surface or be thrown into the air to become airborne.
confusionNotes: Often confused with swallows, but swifts have much more curved, boomerang-shaped wings and never perch on wires or branches like swallows do. Remember: "Swifts are stiff and swift, swallows are graceful and social"—swifts have stiffer wingbeats and don't gather in neat rows on power lines.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, chimney swifts aren't actually related to true swifts found in other parts of the world—they're more closely related to hummingbirds. Many people also don't realize that having swifts nest in your chimney is actually beneficial, as a family can eat thousands of flying insects per day.
compareHints: The chimney swift is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local birds. Compared to other swift family members found elsewhere, chimney swifts are medium-sized and distinguished by their uniform gray coloring and preference for human-built structures over natural cliff faces or tree cavities.
